svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Amazon Cognito identity pools turn a provider token into AWS credentials, and how the two authentication flows differ in where the IAM role is selected. AWS describes Cognito as creating unique identifiers for end users kept consistent across devices and platforms and as delivering temporary, limited-privilege credentials to an application to access AWS resources. Identity pools accept four kinds of authentication artifact: an ID token from an Amazon Cognito user pool, an ID token from OpenID Connect, a SAML assertion from SAML 2.0, and an access token from a social provider, so the social provider case is asymmetric in presenting a bearer credential for an API rather than an assertion about identity. There are two flows for authentication with public providers, enhanced and basic, which reach the same destination while deciding the role in different places. In the enhanced flow the order of operations is GetId then GetCredentialsForIdentity: the application presents proof of authentication in a GetId request, the pool returns an identity ID, the application combines that identity ID with the same proof in a GetCredentialsForIdentity request, and the pool returns AWS credentials. Enhanced authentication manages the logic of IAM role selection and credentials retrieval in the identity pool configuration, the GetCredentialsForIdentity request requests a role based on the contents of an access token, the pool can be configured to select a default role or apply attribute-based or role-based access control, and the credentials are valid for one hour. In the basic or classic flow the order is GetId, GetOpenIdToken, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and the application selects the IAM role that it wants users to assume. GetOpenIdToken returns a new OAuth 2.0 token issued by the identity pool, which is the token AWS Security Token Service evaluates, and this is why trust policy conditions are written against cognito-identity.amazonaws.com and the pool's own aud and amr claims rather than against the upstream provider, whose assertion is consumed earlier and does not reach STS. The central finding is the scope of what a client can then request. AWS states that the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity request in the classic workflow grants the app a greater ability to request credentials for any AWS Identity and Access Management role that has been configured with a sufficient trust policy, and that a custom role session duration can also be requested. The set of roles the client can obtain is therefore not the set the developer intended but the set whose trust policies happen to accept a token from this identity pool, so any role in the account with a loose enough Cognito trust relationship is reachable whether or not anyone thought of it as a mobile app role. AWS is unusually direct about the prerequisites: to implement basic authentication, first evaluate the trust relationships of IAM roles for web identities, then build the logic for role selection into the client and secure the client against modification by users, which is the honest statement that role selection in the client is a decision made on a device the developer does not control. AWS also advises that when creating a new identity pool one should not activate basic classic authentication by default as a best practice, and calls the enhanced flow the most secure choice with the lowest level of developer effort because it reduces the complexity, size and rate of API requests, removes the need for additional requests to AWS STS, has the identity pool evaluate users for the IAM role credentials they should receive, and avoids embedding role selection logic in the client. Crucially the two models cannot be mixed and this is enforced rather than conventional: attempting GetOpenIdToken in an identity pool with role mappings returns the error Basic classic flow is not supported with RoleMappings, please use enhanced flow. Conversely the basic authflow works in pools without role mappings, and AWS describes this type of identity pool as not having a default authenticated or unauthenticated role and not having role-based or attribute-based access control configured. That sentence describes a pool configured for basic-flow use rather than stating a rule, since default authenticated and unauthenticated roles and rule-based role mappings are separate pieces of configuration and an identity pool can have the former without the latter. What matters for the basic flow is that neither of them constrains which roles the client can request, because the application explicitly selects the role for the AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity request and the selected role's trust policy determines whether the request succeeds. The service therefore refuses to allow a configuration that would look authoritative in a console while controlling nothing, which is worth more than the flexibility it removes. On guest access, identity pool trust is configured for Authenticated access, Guest access, or both, and a default IAM role is chosen for authenticated or guest users, so an unauthenticated caller receives credentials from a role rather than none, and a separate IAM role with limited permissions can be defined for guest users who are not authenticated. What separates the two at the IAM layer is the trust policy: AWS states it is important to add the appropriate trust policy for each role so that it can only be assumed by Amazon Cognito for authenticated users in the identity pool, and the example policy allows federated users from cognito-identity.amazonaws.com, restricts the aud of the token, in this case the identity pool ID, to match the identity pool, and specifies that one of the array members of the multi-value amr claim of the token issued by the GetOpenIdToken API action has the value authenticated. The authenticated role is therefore protected from guest tokens by the presence of that amr condition and by nothing else, so omitting it means a guest token satisfies a trust policy written for signed-in users. Two further details matter. Permissions for each user are controlled through IAM roles the customer creates, with rules choosing the role based on claims in the user's ID token, so in the enhanced flow the claims decide server-side while in the basic flow the client decides and claims matter only insofar as a trust policy condition tests them, meaning the same claims have two completely different enforcement points. And granting a user iam PassRole permission to pass a role to the set-identity-pool-roles API allows them to set roles with permissions in excess of their own existing permissions, so the right to configure an identity pool is a privilege escalation path unless the roles that can be passed are constrained. Finally, a Custom developer provider cannot be modified or deleted after the identity pool is created, and in the developer-authenticated flow the claims presented are, from the pool's perspective, arbitrary identifiers whose authentication is authorized by IAM credentials encoded in the application. The recommended audit is to list every IAM role in the account whose trust policy has Federated cognito-identity.amazonaws.com and check two conditions on each: whether the aud is pinned to a specific pool, since a role missing that is reachable from any pool, and whether an amr condition is present, since a role missing that is reachable by guests. Then establish which flow each client uses, because for any client on the basic flow that list is the set of roles it can request rather than the single role the developer had in mind.
svg.title: Two flows, one destination, and the role decided in two different places
svg.text: Both flows end in AWS credentials. Only one of them decides the role server-side.
Amazon Cognito identity pools — and in the other, the trust policy is the whole boundary.
ENHANCED — the pool decides
GetId → GetCredentialsForIdentity
“manages the logic of IAM role selection
and credentials retrieval in your identity pool
configuration”
Credentials “valid for one hour”. No STS call.
AWS: “the most secure choice”.
BASIC (CLASSIC) — your app decides
GetId → GetOpenIdToken → AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
“your application selects the IAM role that
you want users to assume”
Custom session duration. Calls STS directly.
AWS: don't activate it by default.
So what can the client ask for? Not the role you had in mind.
“grants your app a greater ability to request credentials for any AWS Identity and Access Management
role that you have configured with a sufficient trust policy”
The blast radius is every role in the account trusting cognito-identity.amazonaws.com — not the one in your code.
And the honest instruction that comes with it: “secure the client against modification by users”.
The best decision here is a refusal, and it ships as an error string
“Basic (classic) flow is not supported with RoleMappings, please use enhanced flow.”
You cannot configure role mapping that looks authoritative in a console while a client picks its own role.
Default roles and rule-based mappings are separate config — and neither bounds what the basic flow may request.
A guest is still an identity with a role
“Authenticated access, Guest access, or both”,
each with a default IAM role you choose.
One condition separates them: the amr claim
must have the value “authenticated”. Check it.
Same claims, two enforcement points
Enhanced: rules “choose the role for each user
based on claims in the user's ID token”.
Basic: the client chooses; claims matter only
if a trust policy condition tests them.
The audit
List every role whose trust policy has Federated: cognito-identity.amazonaws.com. Two checks each:
is aud pinned to one pool (or is it reachable from all of them), and is there an amr condition (or can guests assume it).
iam:PassRole on set-identity-pool-roles lets someone grant the pool's users more than they hold themselves.
